title: Arjuna drops his bow: work that doesn't cling
hookLine: Arjuna drops his bow and says he'd rather beg; Krishna and the Isha both say keep working, and offer the fruit
carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit
tomorrow: Ajamila's last word: the name at the end
last: IT'S ALL THE LORD'S: ENJOY, DON'T GRAB.

cards: On the morning of the great battle, Arjuna, the finest archer alive, looks across the field and sees his teachers, his cousins, his grandfather. His bow slips from his hand.
Better, he says, to live on alms in this world than to do this. He's ready to quit, and to call quitting the holy choice. His charioteer is Krishna.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION, NOT THE FRUIT.
teach.b: Krishna's answer, in the Bhagavad Gita, isn't fight because you'll win. It's stranger. No one, he says, can stay even a moment without acting.
So the question isn't whether to act, but how. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Don't make the fruit your motive, and don't cling to not acting either.
He names a king who lived it: Janaka and others reached perfection through action itself.

teach.h: A LOTUS LEAF; WATER ROLLS OFF.
teach.b: And he gives an image: whoever acts, offering the work to the Lord and letting go of clinging, is no more stained by wrong than a lotus leaf by water.
That's karma yoga, the yoga of action: do your part fully, and offer what comes of it. The Isha Upanishad says it in a single line.

teach.h: ISHA: WORK, AND LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.
teach.b: Verse two: kurvann eveha karmani, doing works here, jijivishet shatam samah, one may wish to live a hundred years.

teach.h: NA KARMA LIPYATE: ACTION DOESN'T CLING.
teach.b: Then: na karma lipyate nare. Action does not cling to the person. Lipyate means smeared on, sticking, the same verb the Gita uses for the lotus leaf.
Shankara reads the Isha's verse as a concession for those not yet ready to renounce; other teachers hear it as a full path in itself. Either way, the tradition doesn't ask a busy person to leave.
It asks them to change the grip: the work is yours to do well, and the result is offered.

teach.h: DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.
teach.b: That's why many Hindus offer their work before they start it, a short prayer before study, a book touched to the forehead, tools honored once a year at Ayudha Puja.

how: Hindus on the path of karma yoga often describe their work, at home, in a job or in service, as an offering done without clinging to its results, and some teachers cite the Isha's second verse alongside the Bhagavad Gita for this.

o: karma yoga: action done fully, its fruit offered
a debt you pay off by praying every day
rest earned after a lifetime of hard work

games.q: arjuna and the second verse — tap the pairs.
p: drops his bow, wants to beg

s: Krishna tells Arjuna the holy choice is to quit and live on alms
that's Arjuna's idea; Krishna says no one can stay a moment without acting, so act well.
the Isha's second verse and the Gita's lotus leaf use the same verb for clinging
karma yoga means caring only about results
your right is to the action, never to its fruits.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your bow has slipped from your hand, and quitting feels holy. what does Krishna tell you?
o: walk away and live on alms; that's the spiritual path.
act: do your part fully, and offer the fruit.
fight only if you're sure to win.
games.why: your right is to the action, never its fruits. act, and like water on a lotus leaf, it won't cling. the Isha says it too: na karma lipyate.

practice: Think of one piece of work waiting for you: homework, a shift, an email. If you pray, offer it before you start, in any words, to Krishna or to God as you know God. If you don't, offer it to the people it will help.
Picture doing it fully, with care, then setting the result down, the way water rolls off a lotus leaf. Rest with that for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. Krishna and the Isha agree: do your work, offer its fruit, and the action won't cling.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Isha 2: na (not) karma (action) lipyate (clings) nare (to a person). action does not cling to the person.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit. Tomorrow, a man who called his son's name at the end. Until tomorrow.
